bib.title: Introduction to Information Retrieval, Chapter 9: Relevance feedback and query expansion
bib.venue: Cambridge University Press (online edition, draft of April 1, 2009, pp. 177-194)

question: How can a retrieval system help close the vocabulary gap between a query and relevant documents, by using user feedback on documents (local methods) or thesauri and query reformulation (global methods)?

results.claim: Rocchio modified query: move the original query toward the centroid of known relevant documents and away from the centroid of known nonrelevant ones, with weights alpha, beta, gamma.
results.setup: Vector space model (Section 6.3); Eq. 9.3; negative term weights set to 0
results.quote: Starting from q0, the new query moves you some distance toward the centroid of the relevant documents and some dis- tance away from the centroid of the nonrelevant documents.

results.claim: Suggested Rocchio weights give positive feedback more weight than negative: alpha 1, beta 0.75, gamma 0.15.
results.source: Rocchio-family practice, no citation given for the values
results.setup: Eq. 9.3; 'Reasonable values might be'; most systems set gamma < beta
results.quote: Reasonable values might be α = 1, β = 0.75, and γ = 0.15.
results.note: Exercise 9.5 (p. 188-189) uses gamma = 0.25 instead, and Exercise 9.6 uses alpha = beta = gamma = 1. These are exercise settings, not contradictory recommendations.

results.claim: Pseudo relevance feedback (add 20 terms to each query) raised precision at k=50 under lnc.ltc weighting from 64.2% to 72.7%.
results.source: Buckley et al. 1995, Cornell SMART at TREC 4
results.setup: TREC 4 ad hoc, Cornell SMART, lnc.ltc term weighting; pseudo RF adds 20 terms per query; number of topics not stated
results.table: Figure 9.5, row lnc.ltc, columns no RF / pseudo RF (64.2%, 72.7%)
results.note: Table is printed as a figure; numbers 64.2% and 72.7% occur in the text layer.

results.claim: Under Lnu.ltu weighting, pseudo relevance feedback raised precision at k=50 from 74.2% to 87.0%.
results.source: Buckley et al. 1995, Cornell SMART at TREC 4
results.setup: TREC 4, Lnu.ltu (L vs l length normalisation); pseudo RF adds 20 terms per query
results.table: Figure 9.5, row Lnu.ltu, columns no RF / pseudo RF (74.2%, 87.0%)

results.claim: Naive evaluation of RF over the whole collection shows gains of about 50% in MAP, but this is cheating because judged relevant documents are re-ranked higher.
results.setup: Precision-recall before and after one round of feedback, both assessed over all documents in the collection; 'on the order of'
results.quote: gains on the order of 50% in mean average precision.

results.claim: At least five judged documents are recommended for RF to avoid drifting from the information need; one round is often very useful and a second only marginally more.
results.setup: Interactive relevance feedback; no experiment or citation given
results.quote: Accordingly, having at least ﬁve judged documents is recommended.
results.note: The text prints the 'fi' ligature as a single glyph; the quote keeps it.

results.claim: Only about 4% of Excite query sessions used the relevance feedback option, mostly via the 'More like this' link.
results.quote: Only about 4% of user query sessions used the relevance feedback option, and these were usually exploiting the “More like this” link next to each result.

results.claim: About 70% of Excite users looked only at the first page of results; for those who used RF, results improved about two thirds of the time.
results.metric: share of users viewing first page only
results.setup: Excite web search engine; the two-thirds improvement figure is for RF users only
results.quote: About 70% of users only looked at the ﬁrst page of results and did not pursue things any further.
results.note: Two-thirds figure: 'results were improved about two thirds of the time' (same page).

results.claim: Restricting RF to the top 20 prominent terms by term frequency reduces query length and cost; evidence conflicts on whether fewer or more terms give better quality.
results.source: Harman 1992 (fewer terms may be better); Buckley et al. 1994b (more terms better)
results.setup: Long expanded queries are inefficient; 'perhaps the top 20 terms by term frequency'
results.quote: such as perhaps the top 20 terms by term frequency.
results.note: Fig 9.2 example expands the query by 18 terms; Fig 9.5 pseudo RF adds 20 terms.

results.claim: In an early experiment (c. 1960) only 11 of 23 documents indexed under 'toxicity' contained a word with the stem toxi, illustrating the vocabulary gap.
results.setup: Documents properly indexed under the subject toxicity
results.quote: found that only 11 out of 23 documents prop- erly indexed under the subject toxicity had any use of a word containing the stem toxi.

results.claim: Positive feedback is much more valuable than negative; using only the top-ranked nonrelevant document (Ide dec-hi) is the most effective or most consistent variant in some studies, though results are inconclusive.
results.quote: dec-hi is the most effective or at least the most consistent performer.
results.note: In the text layer the term 'IDE DEC-HI' margin label interrupts the sentence; the quote joins the lines.

results.claim: Relevance feedback is mostly a recall-enhancing technique; query expansion generally increases recall but can significantly decrease precision with ambiguous terms.
results.setup: Global thesaurus expansion; example 'interest rate' expanded to 'interest rate fascinate evaluate'
results.quote: However, query expansion may also signiﬁcantly decrease precision, particularly when the query contains ambiguous terms.

results.claim: Overall, query expansion is less successful than relevance feedback, though it may be as good as pseudo relevance feedback; pseudo RF tends to beat global analysis.
results.setup: Qualitative; no comparison numbers in the chapter
results.quote: Overall, query expansion is less successful than relevance feedback, though it may be as good as pseudo relevance feedback.
results.note: Section 9.1.6 (p. 187) says pseudo RF 'tends to work better than global analysis'; Section 9.2.3 (p. 193) says expansion 'may be as good as' pseudo RF. Mildly in tension.

limits: No new experiments: the only numbers are Figure 9.5 (TREC 4, from Buckley et al. 1995), a ~50% MAP figure with no source, the Excite log statistics (Spink et al. 2000) and the 11/23 toxicity anecdote.
Recommended Rocchio weights (1, 0.75, 0.15) and 'at least five judged documents' are given without a citation or setup.
Figure 9.5 does not state the number of topics, the collection size or the pseudo-RF k (number of top documents assumed relevant).
All methods are term-based (vector space, Naive Bayes, co-occurrence thesauri via LSI). Dense retrievers, LLM query rewriting, HyDE, and conversational query rewriting are absent (2008 book; dated).
Web claims are dated: Excite, DirectHit and Yahoo! 2006 interface are historical examples; the claim that RF is little used on the web predates click-model and learning-to-rank practice.
Authors concede that comparisons of RF variants are 'rather inconclusive' and that it is hard to compare performance with and without RF on a residual collection.
The text cache has the Figure 9.6 (Yahoo! screenshot) text as one character per line; it carries no content beyond the caption.
practices: Use Rocchio with positive feedback weighted above negative (gamma < beta), e.g. alpha 1, beta 0.75, gamma 0.15 (p. 183).
Allow positive-only feedback (gamma = 0) or use only the top-ranked nonrelevant document as negative feedback (Ide dec-hi) (p. 183).
Require at least five judged documents and expect one round of feedback to give most of the gain (p. 186).
Limit expansion to prominent terms (e.g. top 20 by term frequency) to keep queries efficient (p. 185).
Evaluate RF on a residual collection, a separate second collection, or by user time-based studies, never on all documents with the judged ones included (p. 186-187).
Use pseudo relevance feedback when no user interaction is possible, and watch for query drift when the top documents are skewed (copper mines / Chile) (p. 187).
Weight added thesaurus terms lower than original query terms (p. 190).
Use a domain-specific thesaurus, since general thesauri give too little coverage (p. 193).
Pair RF with spelling correction; RF alone does not fix misspellings, cross-language or vocabulary-mismatch queries (p. 184).
Prefer implicit feedback (clicks) in high-volume systems: less reliable than explicit but more useful than pseudo RF (p. 187).

terms.definition: In most collections, the same concept may be referred to using different words; it has an impact on the recall of most information retrieval systems.
Techniques for expanding or reformulating query terms independent of the query and results returned from it.
Methods that adjust a query relative to the documents that initially appear to match the query.

Involve the user in the retrieval process so as to improve the final result set: the user marks returned documents as relevant or nonrelevant and the system computes a better representation of the information need.
q_m = alpha q_0 + beta (1/|Dr|) sum of relevant document vectors - gamma (1/|Dnr|) sum of nonrelevant document vectors.
Variant using only the highest-ranked marked nonrelevant document as negative feedback (|Dnr| = 1).
The set of documents minus those assessed relevant, used for the second round of evaluation.
Do normal retrieval, assume the top k ranked documents are relevant, then do relevance feedback as before under this assumption.
Pseudo RF moving the query in the direction of an unrepresentative subset of top documents, e.g. a copper mines query drifting toward Chile.
Using indirect sources of evidence, such as clicks, rather than explicit feedback on relevance.
Using click rates on results as relevance evidence, as in DirectHit.
Users give additional input on query words or phrases, possibly suggesting additional query terms, as opposed to feedback on documents.
From a length-normalised term-document matrix A, C = A A^T gives a similarity score C_uv between terms u and v.
